rows.timeline_year_basis: The Qur'an is never dated; it is the single starting block
rows.name: Qur'an
rows.detail: Partnership recognized, not legislated: 4:12 ('partners in a third', root SH-R-K) and 38:24 ('many of al-khulata' wrong one another'; root KH-L-T, not SH-R-K). AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard 12, al-Tabari and Ma'arif al-Qur'an read al-khulata' as partners; al-Qurtubi calls that reading far-fetched.
rows.detail_long: Who: The Qur'an is the first rung of every USUL ladder: it is never dated, and every later rung refers back to it. What: The Qur'an assumes partnership as social fact — Dawud's parable of wronging partners (38:24) and the inheritance rule making heirs 'partners in a third' (4:12) — without legislating its contract law. Why here: The Qur'an opens the Musharakah ladder and is never dated. Source: Qur'an 38:24; 4:12.

rows.name: Sunan Abi Da'ud 3383
rows.detail: Hadith qudsi: 'I am the third of two partners as long as neither betrays the other.'
rows.detail_long: Who: The Sunan was compiled by Abu Dawud al-Sijistani (817-889); it is the third of the six canonical Sunni hadith collections. Narrator: Abu Huraira. What: Allah declares Himself the third of two honest partners, withdrawing when one cheats. Grading is disputed (a little-known narrator in the chain; al-Hakim graded it sahih; the Gold Ark Library text marks it Sahih). The Prophet also confirmed pre-Islamic partnerships that continued into Islam. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “The Messenger of Allah صلی ‌اللہ ‌علیہ ‌وسلم having said: Allah, Most High, says: I make a third with two partners as long as one of them does not cheat the other, but when he cheats him, I depart from them.” It stands in Commercial Transactions (Kitab Al-Buyu). Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Musharakah ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sunan Abi Da'ud 3383.

rows.name: Bulugh al-Maram 1013
rows.detail: 'I am the third of two partners'. The qudsi charter of partnership: 'I am the third of two partners as long as one does not cheat the other; if he cheats, I depart.'
rows.detail_long: Who: Bulugh al-Maram is one of the hadith collections held in the Gold Ark Library. Narrator: Abu Hurairah. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library (Abu Hurairah): Allah declares Himself the third partner of any two honest partners, withdrawing when either cheats. The moral warranty clause of every shirkah — trust is the capital that keeps God in the venture. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Allah, the Most High, said, 'I am the third (partner) of two partners as long as one of them does not cheat the his companion. Then, if he cheats (his partner) I depart from them.'" .” It stands in Business Transactions. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Musharakah ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year). Source: Bulugh al-Maram 1013.

rows.detail: Partner of the Prophet before Islam. Al-Sa'ib to the Prophet: 'You were my partner in the Ignorance period, and the best of partners — you did not contend or dispute.'
rows.detail_long: Who: Sunan Ibn Majah was compiled by Ibn Majah al-Qazwini (824-887); it is the last of the six canonical Sunni hadith collections. Narrator: al-Sa'ib. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: partnership predates revelation; the Prophet himself traded as a partner before prophethood and is praised for how he behaved in it. Graded Da'eef — kept as colour on continuity of the institution, not as proof. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): You were my partner during the Ignorance period and you were the best of partners, you did not contend or dispute.” It stands in The Chapter on Business Transactions. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Musharakah ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sunan Ibn Majah 2287.

topics_app: Partnership in Farming with Taxpayers and Others and Conditions Between Them

rows.detail: Farming partnership chapter. Imam al-Sadiq permits a farming partnership with a non-Muslim — land/seed/bull from one side, labour from the other, produce split — and polices which side owes which input.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Kafi was compiled by al-Kulayni (864-941), a Persian Shia scholar and hadith compiler. Narrator: Ibrahim al-Karkhi, from Imam al-Sadiq. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: the questioner provides land, seed and bull; the non-Muslim partner works the farm; after the ruler's levy, produce splits one-third / rest. 'It is not unlawful.' When the questioner wants seed repaid off the top, the Imam corrects him: the partnership he formed obliges HIM to provide the seed. Capital-labour partnerships arrive with input obligations already itemised. The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “1. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Sahl ibn Ziyad from al-Hassan ibn Mahbub from Ibrahim al-Karkhiy who has narrated the following: “I once said to abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.), ‘I become a partner of an al-‘ilj (a great non-Muslim person). I provide land, seed, and the bull. Al-‘ilj does the plantation and other works for the farm. When the wheat or barely comes, the produce is divided; al-Sultan takes away his right, one-third is for al-‘ilj and the remaining is for me. [...]” It stands in Partnership in Farming with Taxpayers and Others and Conditions Between Them. Why here: 'Imami reports (Shia line)' rung of the Musharakah ladder; shown at 941 (compilation date: al-Kulayni (d.941, standard reference); report attributed to Imam al-Sadiq). Source: Al-Kafi vol.5, hadith 1013.

rows.name: Ibn Abbas (attrib., Tanwir al-Miqbas)
rows.detail: The earliest attributed gloss on 38:24: 'many partners oppress one another — save those who believe and do good, and they are few.'
rows.detail_long: Who: Abd Allah ibn Abbas (618-686) was a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, remembered as the 'Scholar of the Umma' and highly regarded for his knowledge of traditions and his interpretation of the Qur'an. The commentary Tanwir al-Miqbas is attributed to him by tradition; the attribution is traditional, not critical, which is why the work is marked 'attrib.' What: Tanwir al-Miqbas on the Dawud verse reads khulata' as partners 'and brothers' who 'transgress against one another', excepting the believers who deal rightly — 'those who do not transgress' being few. The Qur'an's own risk warning about partnership, and its exception clause. Attribution traditional, not critical — hence 'attrib.' Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Musharakah ladder; shown at 687 (death of Ibn Abbas, to whom the work is attributed). Source: Tanwir al-Miqbas (attrib. Ibn Abbas), on Q38:24.

rows.name: Ibn Kathir
rows.detail: Ibn Kathir on 38:24: strips the Dawud story of Isra'iliyat embellishment — source criticism applied to the partnership verse itself.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Kathir (1301-1373) of Damascus was a Qur'an commentator, historian and scholar, an expert in tafsir, history and fiqh. A Shafi'i, he is known for a commentary that takes a critical approach to Isra'iliyyat (stories taken from earlier communities). What: Ibn Kathir on 38:24 declines the popular back-story: 'mostly based upon Isra'iliyat narrations. Nothing has been reported about this from the Infallible Prophet that we could accept as true', and grades the one Hadith chain as weak. What survives scrutiny is the verse's own rule — partners wrong each other, except the believers who do right. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Musharakah ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1373 (year of the author's death). Source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, on Q38:24.

rows.name: al-Qurtubi
rows.detail: Al-Qurtubi discusses co-mingling (khultah) and its rules on 38:24 and 4:12.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Qurtubi (1214-1273) was an Andalusian Maliki jurist and Qur'an commentator, taught by the scholars of Cordoba; after the city fell in 1236 he moved to Egypt. His twenty-volume commentary, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an (Tafsir al-Qurtubi), is a general commentary written from a Maliki point of view. What: Al-Qurtubi's treatments of 38:24 and 4:12 work the partnership rules latent in both verses — the wronging partners of Dawud's parable, and the heirs made 'partners in a third' — the co-mingling (khultah) discussion jurists cite for shirkah. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Musharakah ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 1273 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an, on Q38:24.

rows.name: al-Sarakhsi
rows.detail: Al-Sarakhsi splits shirkah into ownership vs contract partnership, with subtypes 'inan, mufawada, abdan, wujuh.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Sarakhsi (1009-1090) was a jurist of the Hanafi school, traditionally known as Shams al-A'imma ('Sun of the Imams'); a saying of the school runs 'when in doubt, follow Sarakhsi'. He is said to have written al-Mabsut while imprisoned. Later Hanafi works, including al-Kasani's Bada'i al-Sana'i, draw heavily on it. What: The Mabsut's fourfold typology — equal-liability mufawada, limited 'inan, labor partnership abdan, credit partnership wujuh — is the classification every later school text and modern standard inherits. In the work itself (near vol. and page 11:150; our literal translation from the Arabic): “And the Messenger of God - may God bless him and grant him peace - was sent while the people were doing that, and he confirmed them in it.” It also states: “(Then) partnership is two kinds: partnership of ownership and partnership of contract. (So partnership of ownership) is that two men share in the ownership of wealth.” It also states: “(And as for partnership of contract,) what is permissible of it is four divisions: mufawada, 'inan, the partnership of faces [wujuh], and the partnership of acceptance [of work].” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Musharakah ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1090 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Mabsut.

rows.name: al-Kasani
rows.detail: Al-Kasani completes the Hanafi doctrine of partnership types.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Kasani (d. 587 AH / 1191 CE) was a jurist of the Hanafi school and author of Bada'i al-Sana'i, a work that draws heavily on al-Sarakhsi's al-Mabsut. What: Bada'i refines the conditions of each shirkah type and the profit/loss rules. In the work itself (vol. and page 6:56; our literal translation from the Arabic): “Partnership in origin is two kinds: partnership of ownerships, and partnership of contracts. And partnership of ownerships is two kinds: a kind that is established by the act of the two partners, and a kind that is established without their act.” It also states: “(And as for) that which is established without their act, it is inheritance, in that the two inherited a thing, so the inherited thing is shared between them as a partnership of ownership.” It also states: “So the partnership of contracts is three kinds: a partnership in wealth, and a partnership in works - and it is called the partnership of bodies and the partnership of the craftsman, and a partnership by acceptance [of work] - and a partnership in faces [wujuh].” It also states: “[Of the partnership in wealth:] it is that two share in a capital, and say: we have become partners in it, on the basis that we buy and sell together, or separately.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Musharakah ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1191 (standard references). Source: Bada'i al-Sana'i.

rows.name: Ibn Rushd
rows.detail: Ibn Rushd supplies the comparative four-school picture of shirkah.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Rushd (1126-1198), known in the West as Averroes, was an Andalusian polymath and jurist of Cordoba who trained in Maliki law and served as a judge. He wrote Bidayat al-Mujtahid on the differences between the schools of law and the principles behind them; his biographer Ibn al-Abbar called him especially competent in the study of juristic disagreement. What: Bidayat al-Mujtahid maps where the schools agree and split on partnership — the comparative lens modern standard-setters still use. In the work itself (vol. and page 4:35; our literal translation from the Arabic): “And partnership, in sum, according to the jurists of the garrison-cities [regions], is of four kinds: the 'inan partnership, the partnership of bodies, the mufawada partnership, and the partnership of faces [wujuh]. One of them is agreed upon, and it is the 'inan partnership.” It also states: “And the three are disagreed upon, and some of their conditions are disagreed upon among those of them who agreed on them.” It also states: “So the Muslims agreed that partnership is permissible in the single kind of coin [al-'ayn] (I mean: dinars, and dirhams).” It also states: “As for when the two partner in two kinds of goods, or in goods and dirhams or dinars, Ibn al-Qasim permitted that, and it is the school of Malik; and it has been said of him that he disliked that.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Musharakah ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 1198 (year of the author's death). Source: Bidayat al-Mujtahid.

rows.name: Yahya ibn Sharif al-Nawawi
rows.detail: Al-Nawawi lists four kinds of partnership and holds that the particular partnership (sharikat al-'inan) 'alone is permitted, provided that the share of each partner is expressly indicated'.
rows.detail_long: Who: Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi (1233-1277), known as Muhyi al-Din, was a Shafi'i jurist and hadith scholar of Damascus. His works include Minhaj al-Talibin and Riyad al-Salihin; al-Asnawi described him as the editor and refiner of the Shafi'i school. What: The standard Shafi'i manual: partnerships of work (abdan), universal partnership (mufawada) and partnership of credit (wujuh) 'are null and void'; only the 'inan partnership is permitted. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Musharakah ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1277 (year of the author's death). Source: Minhaj al-Talibin, Book 13 (Partnership).

rows.name: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi
rows.detail: Ibn Qudama: 'There are four types of copartnership' - of the reins ('inan), of the faces (wujuh), profit-sharing (mudaraba) and of the bodies (abdan).
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi (1147-1223) was a jurist of the Hanbali school who studied in Baghdad and taught in Damascus; he is regarded as one of the school's most authoritative classical figures. He is best known for al-Mughni, a legal encyclopedia that compares the opinions of the Sunni schools while setting out the Hanbali position in detail. He also wrote 'Umdat al-Fiqh. What: The Hanbali primer lists all four types as forms of partnership - unlike the Shafi'i manual, which permits only the 'inan form. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Musharakah ladder, Hanbali voice; shown at 1223 (year of the author's death). Source: 'Umdat al-Fiqh, chapter on Copartnership.

rows.name: Mohammad Nejatullah Siddiqi
rows.detail: 'Diminishing musharakah' engineered for home finance — the ideal profit-and-loss alternative to interest.
rows.detail_long: Who: Mohammad Nejatullah Siddiqi (1931-2022) was an Indian economist (Aligarh; King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah), winner of the King Faisal Prize in 1982 and known for the two-tier mudarabah banking model. What: Siddiqi and colleagues design the declining-balance partnership: bank and customer co-own the house, the customer buys the bank's share out over time while paying rent on the remainder — now the flagship Islamic mortgage. In the source's own words (International Islamic Fiqh Academy (OIC) - Resolution No. 136 (2/15) Diminishing Musharakah and its Shariah Criteria): “Diminishing Musharakah is a new form of relationship involving a partnership between two parties in an income-producing project, and in which one party undertakes to, gradually, purchase the share of the other” “Diminishing Musharakah is characterized by the presence of a binding undertaking from only one party to buy out the share of the other party, provided the latter has the option (to sell or not).” “Diminishing Musharakah is permissible as long as it adheres to the general Shariah rulings on partnerships and to the following conditions:” “The purchase price of the shares should be determined at market value, or a price mutually agreed upon, on the same day of concluding the sale transaction.” Not confirmed by the source read: The page names no person and gives no origin or first use. It does not mention Siddiqi, the 1980s, or home finance. It does not call it 'the ideal profit-and-loss alternative to interest'. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Musharakah ladder; shown at 1980 (1980s). Source: 'Diminishing musharakah' engineered for home finance.

rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 12 (Sharikah and Modern Corporations).
rows.detail_long: Who: AAOIFI (the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions) issues the Shari'ah Standards. They are mandatory in Bahrain, its home jurisdiction, and adopted in the UAE and other countries. What: SS12 maps classical shirkah onto modern corporate forms. Adopted 16 May 2002. Clauses read in the standard's text: 3/1/1/1 sharikah concludes by offer and acceptance, documented and registered where necessary; 3/1/2/1 capital contributed in principle as monetary assets so capital, profit and loss can be determined; 3/1/3/1 each partner is entitled to act in the interest of the partnership. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Musharakah ladder; shown at 2002 (adopted Shari'ah Board meeting 8, Al-Madinah, 11-16 May 2002). Source: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 12 (Sharikah and Modern Corporations).
